Students at Columneetza Junior Secondary School chose Surinderpal Rathor as the mayor of Williams Lake during the mock municipal elections as part of the CIVIX Student Vote program on Oct. 17. Total of 470 schools had submitted their Student Vote results for the 2026 local election, representing 94 municipalities and regional districts throughout B.C. Adults weren’t the only ones heading to the polls over the past two weeks, as Williams Lake students cast mock ballots in both provincial and municipal elections through CIVIX’s Student Vote program. Both local and provincial mock elections ran parallel with real elections in Williams Lake on Oct. 17 and Oct. 24. Four Williams Lake schools participated in the provincial Student Vote: Cataline Elementary, Mountview Elementary, Nesika Elementary and Sacred Heart Catholic School. If students in Williams Lake were deciding the outcome, the BC Greens would lead based on the average vote share across the four schools, with 38.74 per cent, followed by the BC Conservatives at 36.77 per cent and the BC NDP at 24.50 per cent. Williams Lake students were divided in their choices for MLA. At Cataline Elementary, BC Green Party candidate Douglas Gook led with 57.78 per cent of the vote, while Mountview Elementary students favoured BC Conservatives candidate Lorne Doerkson, who received 58.33 per cent of the vote. At Nesika Elementary, BC NDP candidate Kathryn Askee and BC Green Party candidate Douglas Gook tied with 40.91 per cent each. Doerkson also led at Sacred Heart Catholic School with 41.67 per cent. For municipal mock elections in Williams Lake, two schools actively participated in the mock municipal election, Columneetza Junior Secondary School with a 1351 voter turnout, and Nesika Elementary School with 83 voters. A Williams Lake Timberwolves players looks to scored against Quesnel Thunder during the Nightmare on Ice tournament. Williams Lake won the game 5-2. Williams Lake Timberwolves brought home gold with a 4-3 overtime victory over Smithers Storm at the Nightmare on Ice tournament in Quesnel on Sunday, Oct. 25. The tournament began Friday, Oct. 23, with the Timberwolves opening with an 8-1 win over Penticton Jr. Vees. Williams Lake suffered its only loss of the weekend on Saturday morning, falling 7-5 to the Smithers Storm. “Even though we didn’t win, I was really proud of how hard we fought back to make it a close game,” said Mike Bishop, coach of the Williams Lake Timberwolves. Some families stayed in Quesnel, while others travelled back to Williams Lake for Saturday’s 7 a.m. game against Smithers. Bishop said the early start made it difficult for players to get going. The Timberwolves rebounded in the afternoon with a 5-2 win over Quesnel, then advanced to the gold-medal game with an 8-2 semi-final win over Penticton on Sunday, setting up a rematch with Smithers. Williams Lake avenged Saturday’s loss with a 4-3 overtime victory over Smithers. Jaxon Benvin scored the winning goal at 4:04 of sudden-death overtime to secure gold. Bishop told the Tribune how demanding practices, Monday dryland training, and Wednesday spin classes and yoga helped players maintain their energy through a demanding schedule during the weekends. “As the tournament went along, our conditioning proved to be a benefit for the kids,” added Bishop. The physical demands were another challenge for some players experiencing full-contact hockey for the first time. 022534f2cae6a1c81c3ac41a80c51901.text: Artist Tiffany Jorgensen stands on scaffolding in front of her mural, which brings Chilcotin landscape to life in Williams Lake. The mural incorporates resident's memories of Chilcotin through wild horses, wildflowers and familiar landscapes. Tiffany Jorgensen has completed her section of the Cariboo Reflections mural, bringing the Chilcotin landscape to life outside a Williams Lake care home’s dining room. Jorgensen’s work is part of Cariboo Reflections, a collaborative mural on the Cariboo Regional District wall at 108 Third Avenue North. “We are doing a mural from morning to night for the residents of the care home here,” Jorgensen said. “Everybody picked a time of day, which was so funny because it came very organically.” Jorgensen’s section depicts the warm orange light of evening. Her section faces the care home’s dining room, where residents could watch the landscape take shape. Their comments and encouragement provided company while she painted, with one man giving her “the side eye and the thumbs up all the time,” she said. “I went in there and talked to everybody. Everybody is so excited,” Jorgensen said. Sarah Sigurdson, co-founder of Cariboo Art Beat, consulted residents about what they wanted to see. Residents suggested horses, wildflowers, mountains, ranching, logging and gold panning, along with details such as a particular red truck. The artists developed those suggestions into a connected design, Jorgensen explained. Some of the horses in Jorgensen’s newest mural carry more than a connection to the Cariboo landscape. They carry memories of animals that mattered to the people who knew them. Jorgensen asked about horses that had been special to care home residents and incorporated them into the mural, offering a way to honour those memories. She said the gesture drew appreciative responses from people who recognized the horses. Sennecke made it 3-1 at 15:44, deflecting home a point shot for his seventh of the year and Carlsson knocked in a rebound at 18:24 to up the lead to 4-1. Carlsson has four goals so far this season. In the final period, Vancouver pulled within 4-2 at 11:42 when a Ducks clearing attempt hit Boeser and went in behind Dostal. a51f743c5fdb663ceebb10d058650a00.text: Former Finance minister Brenda Bailey is one of several NDP MLAs whose pension was vested on Oct. 23. By waiting until Oct. 24 to hold the B.C. snap provincial election, NDP Leader David Eby saved several of his party’s MLAs from losing their pensions. Had the election been called sooner — and there was plenty of pressure for Eby to do so as the Conservative Party floundered — several outgoing MLAs would have received no pension. Any member of the B.C. legislature first elected on Oct. 24, 2020, and re-elected in 2024 had their pensions vested on Oct. 23, 2026. NDP caucus communications director Edward May says that, from his understanding, pensions were not considered “at all” in timing the election call. “David Eby said the timing was because of the threat to British Columbian jobs and cost of living posed by U.S. tariffs, and the fact that B.C. NDP MLAs were being forced to vote from their hospital beds because one empty seat could have brought the government down,” May said via email. Nine NDP MLAs and three Conservative MLAs had their pensions secured the day before the election, including former Finance minister Brenda Bailey and former Emergency Management minister Kelly Greene, both of whom chose not to run for re-election, as well as Susie Chant and Harwinder Sandhu, both of whom lost. Also passing the threshold were Brittny Anderson, Jennifer Whiteside, Niki Sharma, Josie Osborne and Grace Lore from the NDP, and Lorne Doerkson, Bruce Banman and Trevor Halford from the Conservative Party, all of whom were re-elected. Current pension rules for B.C. legislators date back to 2007. Members of the legislature are entitled to a pension at an annual accrual rate of 3.5 per cent of their highest three-year average of pensionable earnings, capped at 70 per cent. All MLAs must contribute 11 per cent of earnings to the pension fund. MLAs with six years’ service will therefore receive a pension equal to 21 per cent of their top three-year average. 477b7eca0ca3ae9b32b13e9c799e5487.text: The B.C. NDP caucus is meeting this week to select an interim leader to replace David Eby. The B.C. NDP caucus is meeting this week to select an interim leader to replace David Eby, who announced he will step aside after leading his party to an ill-fated snap election. Both outgoing and new members of the legislature plan to meet. “Separately, the party will take a clear and honest look at the campaign and set the timing and process for a leadership race in the weeks and months ahead,” a caucus spokesperson said in an emailed statement. Outgoing Health minister Ravi Kahlon gave a few possible names for interim leader, including Mike Farnworth, who served as Eby’s NDP House leader; Josie Osborne, the outgoing Finance minister; Adrian Dix, a former party leader and outgoing Energy minister; and Niki Sharma, Eby’s attorney general. He also mentioned Ravi Parmar, Spencer Chandra Herbert or Jennifer Whiteside as possibilities. All served as ministers in Eby’s government. “There’s no shortage of very talented people,” said Kahlon, adding that he doesn’t expect the process to be divisive. Kahlon, who chose not to run for re-election, says he planned to focus on his family and wouldn’t consider serving as interim leader. “You never know what will happen in the future, but my focus medium-term is on my family,” he said. “Too early to say,” Parmar said. “I would say that I learned from my mentor in politics, \[former premier\] John Horgan, that before one should act, they should do a lot of listening and learning.” The NDP’s last leadership race was contentious. Eby ran against Anjali Appadurai, but was acclaimed after Appadurai was disqualified for allegedly breaking party electoral rules by working with outside organizations. University of British Columbia political science lecturer Stewart Prest says Eby never really found his stride after that leadership race. “I think it cast a pall over his leadership that he was never able to fully escape,” Prest said. 7b22d77e6c5e18e109b3d5ea75670ce0.text: After a tied vote, a judicial recount, and the drawing of lots, Jennifer Thoss has won election as mayor of the Village of Lytton. The Village of Lytton has a new mayor, after a judicial recount confirmed a tied vote for that position and the decision came down to the drawing of lots. Jennifer Thoss has been confirmed as the incoming mayor, after the recount and draw on Tuesday (Oct. 27). She and incumbent mayor Denise O’Connor each received 45 votes in the municipal election held on Oct. 17, and a recount produced the same outcome. According to CivicInfoBC, there were an estimated 198 eligible voters in Lytton in this election. “Ties are very rare, and only happen once in a blue moon,” said Shannon Story, chief election officer for the Village of Lytton. “But obviously when you’re dealing with a smaller municipality with smaller numbers, a tie is statistically more possible.” As per the Village of Lytton’s election procedure bylaw, and in accordance with the Local Government Act, the tie was referred to a judicial recount in Kamloops. When that recount confirmed the tie, the names of the two candidates were placed in a container, and one was drawn. O’Connor was first elected mayor of the community in 2022, the same year that Thoss was elected for her first term as a councillor there. **News** **B.C. NDP meeting to select new interim leader this week**](https://wltribune.com/2026/10/27/b-c-ndp-meeting-to-select-new-interim-leader-this-week/)

a0a8ca22ee5d6268c687a2e87b672017.text: It came down to a draw, more than a week after the local government election, to determine the final seat in the Princeton town council election. The election was held on Oct. 17, but the vote resulted in a tie for the fourth of four councillor seats. On Oct. 26, Carrie Kassa, chief election officer for Princeton, declared Tyler Willis elected as councillor following a judicial recount lot draw. In the election, held on Oct. 14, Willis and Paula Shackleton were tied for the fourth spot on council, with each receiving 391 votes. Because of the tie, the decision was referred to a judicial recount. This involved recounting the ballots for the two councillors once more. Then, since the vote was still a tie, the winner was determined by a lot draw. This will be third term on council for Willis. He was elected in 2018 and 2022. The others on the Princeton town council are Spencer Coyne as mayor and Barb Gould, Doug Pateman and George Elliott as councillors. Coyne, Gould and Elliott were all members of the past council, while Pateman was a councillor from 2014 to 2018. In the Princeton election, 1,053 ballots were cast. There were an estimated 2,571 eligible voters. Gould finished 690 votes, followed by Pateman with 575 votes and Elliott with 501 votes. The remaining candidates were Amanda Werry with 375 votes, incumbent Randy McLean with 336 votes, Dayton Wales with 325 votes and Chris Obey with 290 votes. In 2008, Marilyn Harkness took the fourth seat on the council with 385 votes, just two more than fifth-place candidate Dina Slowikowski-Campbell. In 2011, Kim Maynard took the fourth spot with 465 votes, just 20 more than fifth-place candidate Ray Jarvis.

419b5d8d1d7c501bac9afa5a1011d810.text: Two ferry sailings are at risk early Thursday amid Georgia Strait wind warning. A dead humpback whale has been reported to the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) near the site where a whale was struck by BC Ferries’ Queen of Surrey from Langdale to Horseshoe Bay terminals on Oct. 18. In an update on Tuesday, Oct. 27, the Marine Education and Research Society said the dead whale was sighted near the Grace Islands just over a week after reports of a ferry striking a whale in the same area. “Necropsy anticipated, but it is believed that external injuries indicate vessel strike,” noted the society. The society says passengers on the ferry saw the whale surface in front of the bow, travelling from right to left. “The whale then surfaced behind the ferry, thrashing, with red visible in the water. Passenger accounts indicate that the ferry did not slow after the collision and that there was no communication to passengers about the impact they felt or what follow-up actions might be taken,” the society said at the time. They said at the time that the strike was likely fatal due to the speed the vessel was travelling and how direct the hit is believed to have been, “however, a fatality may never be confirmed because dead whales often sink to the ocean floor.” In an emailed statement, BC Ferries said they are aware of reports that a deceased whale had been found in the area, and BC Ferries crews also spotted the whale and reported the sighting to Fisheries and Oceans Canada. “This is a very sad development, particularly following the collision involving the Queen of Surrey on Oct. 18. We recognize the concern this raises,” they noted. “At this point, we don’t know whether this is the same whale involved in the collision or what caused its death. We continue to cooperate fully with DFO and will provide whatever information we can to support their assessment.”

Hansen was left paralyzed from the waist down in June 1973 after the vehicle he was riding lost control and rolled west of Williams Lake near Riske Creek. 1e3d3562c55c4dfd617f590d7e2ac905.text: Change may have been in the air across B.C. this fall, but voter turnout certainly wasn’t. This past month, the citizens of the South Cariboo went to the polls twice, first for local municipal elections and then for a snap provincial election. Both elections have resulted in major change. In 100 Mile House, incumbent mayor Maureen Pinkney has been replaced by political newcomer David Jurek, alongside two new councillors. Provincially, our own MLA, Lorne Doerkson, secured re-election and is now the premier-elect, with his party, the Conservative Party of B.C., set to enjoy a majority government with over 60 seats in Victoria. The results of both elections will directly impact our lives and the direction of our community and, in the case of Doerkson, the province for the next four years. Voting’s power was on full display. Yet, voter turnout was not. Here in 100 Mile House, only 40 per cent of eligible voters cast a ballot for mayor and council. Province-wide on Saturday, Oct. 24, around 48 per cent of the electorate cast ballots, down sharply from just over 58 per cent two years ago. When more people choose not to vote than to vote, do we truly have a democracy? Had these people voted, would the outcomes have been the same, or would they have been wildly different? Sadly, we’ll never know. Voter apathy, truly, is the bane of a democratic society. While our first-past-the-post system isn’t perfect, people choosing not to engage with it doesn’t fix it; it just entrenches it. There is a notion among some eligible voters that nothing ever changes and that voting is meaningless. If that were the case, why did our forefathers fight so hard for the privilege? Why do people who don’t live in democratic societies fight for the right to vote? Why do the powerful spend so much money influencing the outcome of elections, if it doesn’t matter? c9de93c1062636154eb2dc8879d3c11d.text: Athletes are arriving in Kelowna for 2026 Skate Canada International (SCI). The best in figure skating across the globe will be competing at Prospera Place Oct. 30 to Nov. 1. Kelowna is the second stop on the SCI Grand Prix series and athletes will be competing for points toward qualification for the Grand Prix Final. Stephen Gogolev is representing Canada in the men’s event. The reigning Canadian champion finished in the top five at both the Olympic Winter Games and the World Championships in his 2025-26 season. In the women’s event, four-time Canadian champion Madeline Schizas will be making her sixth appearance. Two Canadian duos will compete in the pair’s event. Lia Pereira and Trennt Michaud aim for another gold after winning the Nebelhorn Trophy in Germany in September. The reigning junior world champions, Ava Kemp and Yohnatan Elizarov will be making their Grand Prix debut in Kelowna. Canadian couple Marie-Jade Lauriault and Romain Le Gac will be competing in the ice dance event, coming off of a 2026 Canadian Championship bronze medal win. The contest begins Friday, Oct. 30 at 6 p.m. with the men’s short program. The opening ceremony will follow at 7:30 p.m. Medal ceremonies for the men’s and pair’s events will take place at the end of the day on Saturday, Oct. 31. Medal ceremonies for the women’s and ice dance events will take place at the conclusion of the competition on Sunday, Nov. 1. Families are invited to check out Skate Fest Oct. 30-31 outside Prospera Place. The fan event will includes games and activities, vendors, live music and a Halloween treat. Find the event schedule, information on the athletes and tickets by visiting skatecanada.ca.

a464defcbef23fcda7d4c67e816c84f5.text: For the second time, an Armstrong fast food manager has lost an appeal related to his sexual exploitation of a 16-year-old employee. Surjit Singh was 26 years old at the time of the offences, for which he was sentenced to 13 months jail in 2024. After losing an appeal of the conviction back in April, he requested that the B.C. Court of Appeal replace the jail sentence with a conditional sentence served in the community. An appeal court panel dismissed this second appeal, according to a decision released Oct. 2, having found the trial judge made no error in landing on a 13-month jail sentence. Singh became the temporary manager at the fast food restaurant in the summer of 2021. The victim in the case had already worked there for several years and was 15 at the time. Singh knew her age and had researched the age of consent in Canada online. He brought a cake to her home on her 16th birthday. The relationship became sexual, and sexual contact occurred over a two month period at the restaurant, in Singh’s car and in his apartment. The relationship ended when a friend of the victim discovered text messages between her and Singh. The girl’s mother approached restaurant managers and Singh was suspended. He then left the province and was later arrested and brought back to B.C., where he spent eight days in pre-sentence custody. Singh was convicted of sexual exploitation in May 2024. He was acquitted of other charges including sexual assault, as the judge accepted that the relationship was mutual and there was no evidence of grooming. Consent was not at issue in the case; instead it was about Singh’s position of authority. In the April ruling, the court noted Singh held enough control over the victim that “when he wanted to be able to access her cellphone and delete text messages, she let him do that.” It found he had significant control over shift schedules and quantities, and other aspects of the victim’s working life. An Oct. 28 press release from the Kamloops RCMP said the “serious collision” required multiple emergency responders to attend the scene after a car went off the road and down an embankment. “On October 27, 2026, at approximately 6:40 p.m., police received a cell phone crash detection and received multiple reports that a vehicle had gone off Highway 1 near the 3900-block by Cherry Creek,” police said. “The grey Ford Focus was reported to be travelling East on Highway 1 and went off road to the right and then down an embankment of approximately 60ft.” Police noted that Kamloops and Tk’emlúps Rural RCMP detachment frontline officers attended, along with multiple BC Ambulance units, Kamloops Fire Rescue, and New Afton Mine Rescue. BC Highway Patrol also attended to assist with the investigation. Cpl. Dana Napier, spokesperson for the Tk’emlúps Rural RCMP detachment, commented on the incident. “There were five occupants in the vehicle, all five occupants were transported to the hospital where two remain in critical condition,” she said. “The cause of the crash is still being investigated, however, at this time, impairment was not a factor in the crash.” RCMP said anyone who may have been on the highway near the time of the incident and who has dash camera footage of the grey Ford Focus going off-road is asked to contact the Tk’emlúps Rural RCMP detachment at 250-314-1800 and cite file 2026-36059.

72d0cb53d314bf9ecf33a216b0b433c8.text: Darker drives, greater risks: How not ‘falling back’ should change driving habits in B.C. | Williams Lake Tribune Darker drives, greater risks: How not ‘falling back’ should change driving habits in B.C. A B.C.-based safety organization says roads in the province are about to get more dangerous for professional drivers, not to mention motorists who don’t drive for a living. With clocks not “falling back” an hour this weekend, B.C. drivers will spend mornings in more darkness and low light. Road Safety at Work, which aims to improve the safety of people who drive for work or work at the roadside, urges employers and drivers to prepare for reduced visibility and fatigue, and also consider changing their ways this winter. Early Sunday (Nov. 1), B.C. will remain on permanent Daylight Saving Time, meaning sunrise will arrive later this winter. More work trips, morning commutes and school drop-offs will take place in darkness, at a time of year when rain, fog and snow are more common. “Employers need to assess how changing conditions affect workers who drive for work and put appropriate controls in place to reduce those risks,” urges Todd McDonald, head of prevention services at WorkSafeBC. Science says prolonged morning darkness affects natural sleep cycles and may contribute to driver fatigue. Warning signs of fatigue include frequent yawning, difficulty concentrating, drifting within a lane, sore eyes, and difficulty remembering the last few kilometres. “The roads you drive may be familiar but the risks are changing” with permanent Daylight Saving Time, cautions Trace Acres, program director for Road Safety at Work. “In darkness or low light, it’s harder to spot hazards on the road and react.” Employers can help by adjusting schedules that call for driving early in the morning, at night or for long periods, if possible, Acres says. This fall and winter, drivers should slow down when visibility is reduced and leave more distance between vehicles, Road Safety at Work

c466d6f17d5c85b9caf739460559362d.text: Silver Star Mountain Resort has been named the fifth best ski resort in North America in Condé Nast Traveller's 2026 Readers' Choice Awards, published in October 2026. North Okanagan residents know SilverStar Mountain Resort to be a winter paradise rivalling any other. They might be surprised at how many people from far and wide feel the same way about their local ski resort. SilverStar has been ranked fifth among the best ski resorts in North America in Condé Nast Traveller’s 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards, earning a score of 93.26 out of 100. The North American ranking lists 15 resorts. Deer Valley in Utah placed first with a score of 97.78, followed by Sun Valley in Idaho, Vail in Colorado and Whistler Blackcomb in B.C. With Silver Star in fifth, B.C. holds two of the top five places. Mount Washington on Vancouver Island placed ninth, giving the province three resorts on the list. The only other Canadian resort to crack the list was Lake Louise, Alta., which placed 15th. “A village that people live in year-round, alpine runs that still feel like yours on a busy day, and 105 kilometres of pristine Nordic trails. That’s what carries our story further than any campaign could,” said Michael Benedek, executive director of Destination Silver Star. Silver Star’s alpine terrain covers 3,303 skiable acres and 133 runs, with 760 metres of vertical drop. The village sits at 1,609 metres and offers ski-in, ski-out access from its colourful pedestrian village that is home to year-round residents. Silver Star’s Nordic trails connect with Sovereign Lake Nordic Centre to form 105 kilometres of groomed cross-country and skate ski trails, one of the largest combined alpine and Nordic networks in North America. The mountain receives an average of 700 centimetres of snow each year and is 22 kilometres from downtown Vernon in the North Okanagan. 9bd686aa3e9452f593790d4089e035d0.text: The RCMP is seeking public assistance in locating Chelcey Hodder, 43, who is wanted on Canada-wide warrant for failing to return to a facility as ordered. Hodder has been missing since Oct. 23, and is believed to be in the Hope area or travelling to Kamloops. Coquitlam RCMP is asking for the public’s help in locating a woman wanted on a Canada-wide warrant who is believed to be in the Hope or Kamloops areas. Chelcey Hodder, 43, was last seen at 2:30 p.m. in the area of ƛ̓éxətəm Regional Park in Coquitlam on Oct. 23. She is wanted on a warrant of committal after failing to return to her facility as ordered. The Coquitlam RCMP Investigational Support Team tracked Hodder to Hope, and it is believed she is either still in the Hope area or is travelling to Kamloops. The police say to not approach Hodder if she is seen. Anyone who has seen Hodder or knows of her whereabouts is asked to contact their local RCMP detachment and reference Coquitlam RCMP file number 2026-27834.

f9f482bad9d48919f8e82c06687be5a6.text: A Forest Grove man was arrested for stabbing another on Monday, Oct. 26. 100 Mile House RCMP Sgt. Brian Lamb said police responded to a report of an assault with a weapon at a residence on Bakken Road in Forest Grove. On arrival, officers determined an adult male had been stabbed. Lamb said a second adult male was located in the residence and arrested. “The victim was assessed at the scene by Emergency Health Services and transported to hospital for further treatment,” Lamb said. “The injuries sustained were serious but not believed to be life-threatening.” During their response, RCMP executed a search warrant to search the residence for any additional evidence. As for the suspect, Lamb said he was held in custody pending a bail hearing. “Both men were known to each other, and this was not a random act,” Lamb stated. This incident was one of 91 calls for service RCMP responded to between Oct. 19 and Oct. 26. A vehicle believed to have been stolen sometime in the last several months was reported to police last week. On Oct. 20, Lamb said a 2001 white Chevrolet Tahoe was reported stolen from a property along the 7000 block of Caroline Road. It is unknown when the vehicle, which did not have any license plates attached, was taken. An ATV hauling a trailer full of building material was reported on Oct. 20. Lamb said the ATV was travelling along Horse Lake Road, with officers locating and stopping the vehicle at the 5000-block of Horse Lake Road. After talking with the male driver, Lamb said officers determined he was prohibited from driving. “The male was arrested and later released to attend court at a future date,” Lamb said. “The ATV was impounded and the male was also served a violation ticket for no insurance.” Sometime overnight on Oct. 22, a commercial property was broken into on Horse Lake Road.
